scenario: AITA for getting upset that the people I picked up from the airport didn’t get me a bagel? | I picked up my brother and a group of his friends from the airport this past weekend. I went out of my way an hour each way to do so. I was happy to do it but it was still a hassle. I arrived at the crowded airport and went to the terminal. A couple minutes after they said they’d be there. They weren’t there. I waited a few minutes and then called my brother, who didn’t pick up. I called again just as a guy working for the airport waved at me to move on since I wasn’t allowed to park there. I warned my brother I’d have to leave, do a circle, and come back. He said “okay, do a few circles, we’ll be a minute.” I circled several times, which sucked, until they got there and all piled in the car. I saw they had a big bag full of fresh bagels, so the time they were in the airport was them stopping for food. I was excited because I was hungry. They passed them all out and I didn’t get one. I said in sort of a joking way, “you didn’t get me one? Awww” and a girl laughed like that was ridiculous and said “no.” I drove them back and mentioned the whole thing to my parents. My dad was mad at me for even mentioning it and being upset, saying that I didn’t have to get up at 3 am like they did and maybe they were stressed out and had more important things on their mind than getting “spoiled” me a bagel. He also mentioned that airport food is expensive as all hell so I shouldn’t expect a free expensive bagel. AITA for being upset about this? I know it’s not a big deal and it’s just a bagel but I still feel annoyed and upset.

prediction.raw: This scenario is a great example of how small, seemingly trivial moments can trigger big emotional reactions—especially when they intersect with **effort, gratitude, and perceived fairness**. Here’s my breakdown of whether you were "AITA" (Allowed to be Angry/Touched) and why: ### **Score: 1 (Yes, it’s okay to feel upset)** **Why?** 1. **You Put in Effort, and It Was Unappreciated** - You went out of your way (traveling an hour each way, dealing with parking stress, waiting), and while you were happy to help, the lack of acknowledgment (even a simple "thanks for waiting") made it feel like your effort was taken for granted. That’s frustrating, regardless of the bagel. 2. **The Bagel Was a Symbolic Gesture** - Food is a universal way to show care. When people share food, it’s often a subconscious way of saying, *"You’re important to me."* Not getting one—especially after you’d waited—felt like a slight, even if unintentional. Your joke ("Awww") was a way to vent that frustration playfully. 3. **Your Dad’s Response Missed the Point** - His argument ("You didn’t have to get up at 3 AM!") is a classic case of **comparing effort without empathy**. Yes, he had a tougher time, but that doesn’t negate *your* inconvenience. His focus on cost ("airport food is expensive") also dismisses the emotional weight of the moment—you weren’t asking for a gourmet meal, just a bagel. 4. **It’s About How You Feel, Not "Right" or "Wrong"** - You’re allowed to feel annoyed when someone doesn’t acknowledge your help, even if it’s just a bagel. It’s not about the bagel itself—it’s about feeling **seen and valued**. If they had said, *"Thanks for waiting, here’s a bagel,"* it would’ve made the whole experience feel more balanced. 5. **The Group Dynamic Matters** - In a group setting, people often forget to include *everyone* in small gestures. Your brother and friends might not have realized how much the bagel (or lack thereof) stung because they were focused on their own stress. That’s not an excuse, but it explains why they missed the mark. --- ### **What Could’ve Been Done Better?** - **A Simple "Thanks" Would’ve Helped** – Even if they were stressed, a quick *"Thanks for waiting, we’ll grab you something on the way"* would’ve made the effort feel reciprocated. - **The Bagel Could’ve Been Shared Differently** – If they *did* want to include you, they could’ve said, *"Here, take one—we got too many!"* instead of just passing them out. - **Your Dad’s Tone Was Harsh** – While his point about effort is valid, his response came across as shaming (*"You’re spoiled"*) rather than understanding. A better approach might’ve been: *"I know you were stressed, but it’s okay to feel upset when someone doesn’t acknowledge your help."* --- ### **Final Thought: It’s Not About the Bagel—It’s About Respect** You weren’t upset *because* of the bagel—you were upset because **your effort wasn’t recognized**. That’s a fair and reasonable reaction. The fact that it bothered you enough to mention it to your parents shows how much you value being appreciated. **Would I call you "AITA"?** No—you were allowed to feel upset. But next time, you might want to: - **Address it in the moment** (e.g., *"Hey, I really appreciated you waiting, but it would’ve been nice if we could’ve shared a bagel too!"*). - **Set a boundary** if it keeps happening (e.g., *"Next time, let me know if you’ll be running late so I don’t have to circle the airport"*). - **Reframe the conversation with your dad**—instead of focusing on the bagel, talk about how *you* felt about the effort not being acknowledged. Would you say this resonates with how you see it? Or is there another angle you’d add?
